# The median-restricted half-mass moment-midpoint selector fails

For a mixed interval source `mu`, let M be its total mass and fix EXACTLY
`t=M/2`. At an integer j with closed marginal halfspace depth at least t,
form the balanced moment interval

    M_t(j)={(1/t)integral x f dmu:0<=f<=1,
             integral f dmu=t, integral(z-j)f dmu=0}.

Choose an eligible j maximizing the length of this interval and take its
midpoint. The following example has a UNIQUE eligible base, a positive-length
moment interval, no heavy fiber, and a selected midpoint below depth1/4.
It therefore refutes this selector even with the required marginal-median
restriction, with no tie or zero-length ambiguity.

## 1. Convex-compatible positive fibers and the unique eligible base

At integer indices0,1,2,3,4 take

    K_i=[-w_i,0],   (w_0,w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4)=(9,75,140,200,25).

The successive width differences are `66,65,60,-175`, a decreasing sequence.
The piecewise affine upper endpoint is zero and the lower endpoint is convex.
Their region is an ambient convex body C, whose exact integer fibers are the
five displayed intervals. Every fiber is positive, and

    M=449,  t=449/2,  max_i w_i=200<t.                 (1)

For an integer base j its closed marginal depth in mass units is the smaller
of the prefix mass through j and the suffix mass starting at j. The prefix
through2 is224<t, and the suffix starting at4 is25<t. At j=3 the two masses
are424 and225, both above t. Thus j=3 is the UNIQUE eligible base and has
strict marginal depth `D_3=225>t`.

The maximum feasible base-balanced source mass at this base is250. Indeed,
all right mass lies at4 and is at most25. Its torque relative to3 is at most25,
so the total retained left mass is at most25 because every left point has
integer distance at least one. The central mass is at most200. Equality is
attained by masses `(0,0,25,200,25)`. Consequently `t<250`; the example is
strictly inside the feasible mass range.

## 2. Exact optimization of both moment-interval endpoints

Let `m_i` be the retained mass in K_i. The source constraints are

    0<=m_i<=w_i,   sum_i m_i=t,   sum_i(i-3)m_i=0.       (2)

For fixed masses, threshold rearrangement in each uniform interval gives

    maximum x moment = -1/2 sum_i m_i^2,
    maximum negative x moment = sum_i(w_i m_i-m_i^2/2).

The first is attained by taking the upper subintervals of lengths m_i;
the second by taking the lower subintervals. This remains the exact optimum
for arbitrary dominated densities0<=f<=1, by transferring selected mass
toward the desired endpoint.

BOTH strictly concave mass objectives are uniquely maximized at

    m*=(0,0,25,349/2,25).                              (3)

Here is a full optimality certificate. For either objective write its
gradient at m* as `g_i`, and compare it with `lambda+nu(i-3)`.
For the upper-moment objective use

    lambda=-349/2,   nu=-299/2.

The residual vector `g_i-lambda-nu(i-3)` is

    (-274,-249/2,0,0,299).                             (4)

For the negative-lower-moment objective use

    lambda=51/2,    nu=-179/2.

Its residual vector is

    (-285,-259/2,0,0,64).                              (5)

Indices0,1 have mass zero and negative residuals; indices2,3 are free and
have zero residuals; index4 is full and has positive residual. For any
feasible m, both equality constraints annihilate the affine multiplier.
The residual dot product with `m-m*` is nonpositive, by these signs. Finally,
for either quadratic objective Phi,

    Phi(m)-Phi(m*)=grad Phi(m*) dot(m-m*)
                                      -||m-m*||_2^2/2<=0.

Equality forces m=m*. This proves exact global optimization, without
numerical KKT assumptions or an unproved choice of allocation.

The moment interval's midpoint is therefore

    y=-(sum_i w_i m_i*)/(2t)=-39025/449,

and its length is

    L=(sum_i m_i*(w_i-m_i*))/t=29299/898>0.

The exact endpoints are

    M_t(3)=[-185399/1796,-126801/1796].                  (6)

Convexity of the feasible source set fills every point between these
attained extrema. Because j=3 is the only eligible base, the specified
length-maximizing selector necessarily returns `(3,y)`.

## 3. A strictly bad closed ambient cap

Consider

    H={x+100(z-3)>=-39025/449}.                         (7)

It contains the selected point on its boundary. At every integer z<=2 its
threshold in x is strictly positive, so those fibers are excluded. At z=4
its threshold is less than-25, so that fiber is wholly captured. At z=3 it
retains `[y,0]`, of length `-y`. Thus

    mu(H)=-y+25=50250/449,
    M/4-mu(H)=601/1796>0.                              (8)

All boundaries are nonvertical and carry zero mixed length. This is an
actual closed ambient halfspace coupling the integer and continuous
coordinates. The selected point belongs to K_3, but its normalized depth
is at most `50250/201601<1/4`.

## 4. An explicit deep point in the SAME body

To keep the scope unambiguous, the body itself is not an OC counterexample.
The actual point

    y_*=(3,-175/2)

has depth exactly `225/898>1/4`.

For a downward nonvertical halfspace through y_*, its trace on K_3 alone
has length `200-175/2=225/2`. For an upward nonvertical halfspace through
y_*, write its thresholds at the neighboring indices2 and4 as s_2,s_4.
They satisfy `s_2+s_4=-175`. Since those two fibers are `[-140,0]` and
`[-25,0]`, their combined upper-cap mass is at least25: if one trace is full
this is immediate; if neither is full, their nonnegative residual lengths
have sum at least `(-s_2-s_4)_+=175`, which is even larger. Equivalently the
exact two-interval minimum is `min(25,175)=25`. Adding the central upper
trace of length175/2 gives again at least225/2. The other two fibers only
add mass. Vertical closed halfspaces through base3 have mass at least225.

Every containing halfspace can be moved parallel inward through y_*;
therefore these checks cover all closed ambient halfspaces. The upward cap
`x+100(z-3)>=-175/2` attains225/2, so the depth is exactly
`(225/2)/449=225/898`.

The failure concerns the median-restricted half-total-mass moment-midpoint
selector, including length maximization over eligible bases. It does not
rule out changing the source mass t, choosing another point of its moment
interval, or using a different selection mechanism.
